newsitem.title: UK: Will UK Labour pay price for being defensive?.
newsitem.headline: Will UK Labour pay price for being defensive?.

text.p: After three weeks of testing enemy battle lines, the two main armies in Britain's election campaign are finally on the move.

The fight for power has intensified considerably this week, at the half-way stage in the campaign, coinciding with tentative opinion poll evidence that the ruling Conservatives have checked and may be pushing back the advance of their Labour opponents.
Certainly, the mood in the Conservative camp has brightened as the ruling party's guns start to find their range.
In Birmingham on Tuesday, Prime Minister John Major snapped at a reporter who asked him about sleaze allegations against former Conservative trade minister Neil Hamilton.
He accused another of trying to lay a bear trap for him and later sounded in valedictory mood when he confided that he thought quashing inflation would be his greatest legacy.

But by Wednesday night, on a flight back from a day on the stump in Wales, he was chatting animatedly with journalists after hearing that a MORI poll had shown the Conservatives narrowing Labour's lead to 15 points from 27 points in a week.
And at Thursday's daily news conference he breezily promised to be still there answering questions in five years' time.
While Major has rediscovered a spring in his step, Labour leader Tony Blair is being forced onto the back foot.

He was as confident as ever during a hard day's campaigning in western England on Wednesday but has looked uneasy this week when grilled in high-profile BBC television and radio interviews and at his daily news conferences.
Deputy Prime Minister Michael Heseltine gleefully claimed Blair was cracking under the strain of explaining apparent policy shifts over privatisation and union rights.

Some commentators say Labour is paying the inevitable price of its ultra-cautious strategy of ditching any controversial policies in order to persuade floating voters it can be trusted with power again after being in the wilderness since 1979.
"Logical enough: but it means that the party which ought to be challenging are behaving like the incumbents, and the party of 18 years in office are attacking like Opposition terriers.

"Labour is standing there holding its popularity with Middle England like some huge, rare and infinitely fragile glazed pot, which might crash to the ground if it attempts to move a muscle," Andrew Marr wrote in The Independent newspaper.
He urged Labour's "clenched-buttock" strategists to stop being timid. "This business of trying to offend nobody is unsustainable," he said.
Labour insiders say they had expected their poll lead to narrow, but Blair acknowledged on Thursday that he had to prevent the Conservatives from gaining momentum.

Ordering a copy of Labour's 10-point "contract with the British people" to be sent to every household in the country, Blair said: "The Tory Lie Machine is now moving up a gear, so it is vital that we move up a gear in our positive campaigning. The contract is the key to that."
He remains convinced that Labour's positive message that it can be trusted to carry out a limited but achievable agenda of change will be heard in the din of battle.
The polls are still very much in his favour. Even on MORI's figures, Blair would have a thumping majority of about 175 in the 659-seat House of Commons, the lower chamber of parliament.
No party has ever come back from such a deficit, which other surveys, including a Gallup poll in Thursday's Daily Telegraph, suggest is even wider.
Politics professor Anthony King said that despite the sound and fury almost nothing seemed to have changed since the campaign began three weeks ago.
The Conservatives, according to Gallup, remain 23 points behind Labour. Three weeks before polling day in 1992 they were two points ahead.
"The contrast between the two parties' relative standings at this stage of the 1992 general election campaign could hardly be more vivid," King commented.
